title: Trigger-Based Invocation
explain: When I have lots of time-based work, like lease expiry checks, periodic jobs and one-off scheduled tasks, I do not give each its own sleeping thread. I keep a priority queue of next trigger time and task, with one timer loop that sleeps until the earliest, pops what is due, and pushes it to a worker pool. The loop only decides when, never does the work.
model:
**Don't:** N coroutines or threads each sleeping until their time. That costs memory per waiter, makes cancel and reschedule awkward, and collapses at hundreds of thousands of items (500,000 threads x 1 MiB of stack is about 488 GiB of address space).

**Do:** `PQ((next_trigger_time, task))` plus one loop. (User's framing: do not make threads wait; compute the due time, queue it, pop at the time, push into the Running queue.)

```
loop:
  peek earliest (t, task)
  sleep until t   (or until woken by an earlier insert)
  pop everything now due
  push each to Running queue (worker pool)
  recurring tasks: compute next time, re-insert
```

Details that matter:

- **Wake on earlier inserts**, or the new task fires late.
- **Fixed rate** (`scheduled + interval`) keeps cadence; **fixed delay** (`finish + interval`) stretches by the runtime. Decide on missed triggers: skip, coalesce, or run all.
- **Structure:** heap is O(log n); a [timer wheel](#/sd/f/timer-wheel) is O(1) with coarse precision.
- **Several instances:** give each task one owner ([lease](#/sd/f/lease) or hash) and make tasks idempotent.
- **Durability:** store `next_trigger_time` in the DB ([time-box patterns](#/sd/f/time-box-patterns)).
- It is the Wait side of [wait / running queues](#/sd/f/wait-running-queues).

details.q: Why not one sleeping thread or coroutine per scheduled item?
details.a: Memory per waiter, awkward cancellation and rescheduling, and it breaks at scale: 500,000 lease checks as threads with a 1 MiB stack each reserve about 488 GiB. One timer loop plus a priority queue holds the same schedule in a few megabytes.

details.q: The loop sleeps until 12:00:00 and a task due 11:00:05 is inserted. What must happen?
details.a: Wake the loop (condition variable signal, or re-arm the timer) so it recomputes the earliest due time. Otherwise the new task fires at 12:00:00, nearly an hour late.

details.q: A job should run every 10 s but is configured fixed-delay and each run takes 4 s. How often does it start?
details.a: Every 14 s, about 257 starts per hour instead of 360. Use fixed rate (`scheduled_time + interval`) if cadence matters, and decide what to do if a run overruns the interval.

details.q: What do you do about triggers missed during downtime?
details.a: Choose per task: skip them, coalesce into a single catch-up run, or run every missed one. Billing wants exactly the missed runs; a cache refresh wants one catch-up. Make it an explicit policy.

details.q: Three scheduler instances each load 'nightly billing at 02:00'. What happens?
details.a: It runs about three times. Give each task a single owner (a lease or leader per task, or hash tasks across instances) and make the job idempotent as a backstop.

A heap is exact and O(log n) per insert and cancel, fine up to hundreds of thousands. A [timer wheel](#/sd/f/timer-wheel) is O(1) with tick-level precision, suited to millions of timeouts such as heartbeat leases.

details.q: How do triggers survive a restart?
details.a: Persist next_trigger_time (and attempt state) in the database, and rebuild the in-memory queue on startup; overdue entries simply fire immediately according to the missed-trigger policy.

prompts.q: Explain the trigger-based approach and why it beats sleeping threads.
points: Priority queue of next trigger time and task
One timer loop sleeps until the earliest
Pops due items and pushes to the worker pool
Recurring tasks re-insert with a new time
Threads per waiter cost memory and do not scale

prompts.q: Walk through the details that make a timer loop correct.
points: Single owner per task across instances, idempotent jobs

prompts.q: Choose between a heap and a timer wheel for 2 million heartbeat timeouts.
points: Wheel O(1) insert and cancel, tick precision
Millions of timeouts with approximate firing: wheel
